clue.text: A bad pain after degree for priestesses

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held: 'A bad pain after degree for priestesses'. BAC (degree) and an anagram of ACHE ('bad pain') give BACCHAE, but no clue word supplies THE; 'A' would have to stand for THE, so the parse is incomplete as printed.
annotationWithheld.clue: A bad pain after degree for priestesses

clue.text: Said to weary in Shakespearian principality

indicators.note: said signals that the word for weary is spoken, giving a sound rather than a spelling

parts.note: to weary someone is to tire them

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on growing weary in one of Shakespeare's realms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Said' turns TIRE into its sound-alike, TYRE; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Pericles is Prince of this Phoenician city in Shakespeare's play Pericles, Prince of Tyre.

clue.text: Judge as lefthanded regicide

definitions.meaning: one of the leaders of Israel in the biblical Book of Judges
a left-handed man who killed a king

explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Judges this left-handed Benjamite judged Israel after stabbing King Eglon of Moab with a dagger hidden on his right thigh.

clue.text: Lent partly for Eliot's period of mourning

definitions.meaning: a single day forming part of the season of Lent
a penitential poem by T. S. Eliot

explanation.definitionFit: The penitential day that opens Lent gave its name to T. S. Eliot's 1930 poem of repentance and grief.

clue.text: Roughly about hotel conspirator

indicators.note: about signals that the abbreviation for roughly is placed around the word for hotel

parts.note: CA, short for circa, means roughly
an inn is a hotel

explanation.surface: A vague report of a plotter loitering near a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: CA (circa) goes 'about' INN to give C-INN-A.
explanation.definitionFit: In Julius Caesar, Cinna is one of the conspirators who plot the assassination of Caesar.

clue.text: He made Abraham swear — possibly called him a celeb

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of the phrase him a celeb are one possible rearrangement of the name

explanation.surface: A man who forced the patriarch to take an oath might have hailed him as a celebrity.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis 21 the king of Gerar has the patriarch take an oath of fair dealing at Beersheba.

clue.text: Bad news for book collectors — new dues for what's secondhand

indicators.note: new signals that the letters of dues are made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A secondhand copy disappoints a book collector, who must still pay dues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges DUES. The opening phrase is colour: a used copy is bad news to a collector who wants mint condition.
explanation.definitionFit: A secondhand item has already been owned and worn by someone else.

clue.text: Underfed tailor to inform about travel arrangement

indicators.note: about signals that the word for inform is placed around the rearranged letters

parts.note: to sing is slang for informing on someone to the police

indicators.note: arrangement signals the letters of travel are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A hungry tailor is asked to report on travel plans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underfed tailor' is Starveling, one of the amateur actors in A Midsummer Night's Dream; 'sing' is slang for informing to the police, and 'arrangement' rearranges travel.
explanation.definitionFit: Robin Starveling, the thin tailor among Shakespeare's mechanicals, has a name meaning a half-starved creature.

clue.text: Like diggers and seekers, they don't agree

definitions.meaning: the Diggers and Seekers were radical religious groups of seventeenth-century England, outside the established church
people who disagree with an accepted view

explanation.definitionFit: Nonconformists who refused the Church of England, like the Diggers and Seekers, were called by this name for those who disagree.

clue.text: Clemens version of Hard Times?

parts.note: Samuel Clemens, as Mark Twain, wrote a travel book whose title is an idiom for enduring hard living, as if his answer to Dickens

explanation.surface: A question whether Samuel Clemens rewrote the Dickens novel Hard Times.
explanation.walkthrough: Hard Times looks like Dickens's title, but here it means a life of hardship, which Twain's 1872 book of Western travels names in an idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Living without comforts is an idiom for hard times, and Twain's book of that title recounts his rough years in the West.

clue.text: Lewis seems to have given her a way through the woods

definitions.text: Lewis seems to have given her a way through the woods

parts.words: Lewis seems to have given her a way through the woods
parts.note: Sinclair Lewis named a novel after a hero whose surname is timber plus lane, a way through woods

explanation.surface: A novelist seems to have shown a woman a path through a forest.
explanation.walkthrough: Sinclair Lewis's novel Cass Timberlane: TIMBER + LANE is 'a way through the woods', so Lewis appears to give it to the title character as a surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Sinclair Lewis's 1945 novel bears the forename Cass and a surname built from timber and lane.

clue.text: International group gets DNA sequence and a short drink in Pushkin's work

parts.note: EU, the European Union, is an international group of countries
a gene is a sequence of DNA
a means one
gin is a short, a spirit served in a small measure

explanation.surface: A European body receives genetic material and a quick tot of spirits while reading Russian literature.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a 'short' is a small measure of spirits as opposed to beer, so a short drink is GIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Pushkin's novel in verse is named after its hero, the Russian dandy Eugene.

clue.text: A tight ship run by Rimbaud?

definitions.text: A tight ship run by Rimbaud?

parts.words: A tight ship run by Rimbaud?
parts.note: tight means drunk, so the ship is a drunken boat, the title of a famous Rimbaud poem

explanation.surface: Asks whether the poet Rimbaud was a strict captain who ran a tight ship.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'run a tight ship' means to keep strict order, but tight here is slang for drunk: Rimbaud's poem title translates as The Drunken Boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Rimbaud's 1871 poem, in French, means The Drunken Boat, and tight is slang for drunk.

clue.text: Changes by Muir on meat item he made unrecognizable

definitions.text: by Muir on meat item he made unrecognizable
definitions.meaning: Edwin Muir's first poetry sequence is titled with this word followed by on a Time Theme, and those last three words are the letters of meat item he rearranged

explanation.definitionFit: Variations are changes, and Edwin Muir's 1934 sequence is Variations on a Time Theme, whose last words rearrange 'meat item he'.

clue.text: "Even I may be concealing an angel within" suggests Longfellow poem

indicators.note: concealing signals that the rearranged letters hide the word angel inside them
may be signals that the letters of even I are only one possible arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The quotation suggests even the speaker may harbour an angel inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' rearranges 'Even I' around ANGEL, which 'concealing' places inside; 'an', 'within' and 'suggests' only tie the surface together.
explanation.definitionFit: Longfellow's 1847 narrative poem follows an Acadian girl separated from her lover during the expulsion.

clue.text: A mountain of it created by Enid Blyton

definitions.text: A mountain of it created by Enid Blyton

parts.words: A mountain of it created by Enid Blyton
parts.note: Enid Blyton wrote a children's series with titles such as The Mountain of, The Island of and The Castle of the same word

explanation.surface: Enid Blyton produced a huge heap of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A mountain of' looks like 'a great deal of', but it is the title The Mountain of Adventure, one of Blyton's Adventure series of children's books.
explanation.definitionFit: Blyton's eight-book children's series includes The Mountain of Adventure, published in 1949.

clue.text: Not decided, like Mill's questions in his essays on political economy

definitions.text: like Mill's questions in his essays on political economy
definitions.meaning: John Stuart Mill published Essays on Some ... Questions of Political Economy in 1844

explanation.definitionFit: An open matter is one still unresolved, and Mill titled his 1844 economics essays after such open questions.

clue.text: Applause for brilliant success

explanation.definitionFit: The French loan word means both acclaim and a dazzling triumph or flourish.

clue.text: Elsie, who got the pip from Hay

definitions.text: Elsie, who got the pip from Hay

parts.words: Elsie, who got the pip from Hay
parts.note: Ian Hay's novel Pip has a heroine named Elsie who is courted by its hero Pip

explanation.surface: A woman named Elsie was irritated by something called Hay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got the pip' looks like the slang for being annoyed, but Pip is the hero and title of Ian Hay's novel, and Elsie is the girl he wins.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of Elsie, the heroine whom the hero Pip wins in Ian Hay's 1907 novel.

clue.text: Olive, reported philanthropist, was one of those who recount dreams

indicators.note: reported signals that the word for a philanthropist is heard rather than read

parts.note: a Shriner is a member of the fraternal order famous for charitable children's hospitals

explanation.surface: A woman called Olive, said to be a benefactor, told of her dreams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reported' turns SHRINER into its sound-alike. The last phrase points to Olive Schreiner's 1890 book of allegories called Dreams.
explanation.definitionFit: Olive is the first name of the South African novelist who wrote The Story of an African Farm and Dreams.

clue.text: "… what branches grow / Out of this stony rubbish?"

definitions.text: "… what branches grow / Out of this stony rubbish?"

parts.words: "… what branches grow / Out of this stony rubbish?"
parts.note: lines from the opening section of Eliot's 1922 poem, describing a barren wilderness

explanation.definitionFit: The quotation comes from The Burial of the Dead, the first section of Eliot's 1922 poem of a barren wilderness.

clue.text: Substitute found in Belloc, umpteen times

indicators.note: found in signals the letters sit within the run of words Belloc, umpteen

explanation.surface: A stand-in is discovered countless times in the writings of Belloc.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is belLOC UMpteen; 'times' is a link completing the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor or cleric standing in temporarily for another is a stand-in.

clue.text: Spring's stimulus

parts.note: Howard Spring wrote a novel whose title says this thing is the spur, quoting Milton's Lycidas

explanation.surface: Whatever spurs the season of spring into life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like the season, but it is the novelist Howard Spring, whose Fame Is the Spur names the stimulus.
explanation.definitionFit: Howard Spring's 1940 novel declares renown to be the spur, quoting Milton's Lycidas.

clue.text: Like Jerome's ideas

parts.note: Jerome K. Jerome published ... Thoughts of an ... Fellow in 1886

explanation.surface: Describing the notions of a man called Jerome.
explanation.walkthrough: Jerome K. Jerome's essays are Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow, so his ideas are described by this word.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerome K. Jerome's essay collection calls his thoughts lazy and unoccupied.

clue.text: Like poem in good icon

indicators.note: in signals that the letters lie inside the phrase good icon

explanation.surface: A likeness of a poem appears within a fine religious image.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes something of or like an ode, a lyric poem.

clue.text: "Marking certain things as low and" (Tom Brown's Schooldays)

definitions.text: "Marking certain things as low and" (Tom Brown's Schooldays)

parts.words: "Marking certain things as low and" (Tom Brown's Schooldays)
parts.note: the quotation from Thomas Hughes's school novel breaks off before its final word, which completes it

explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hughes ends the phrase with a word for low, villainous or dishonourable conduct.

clue.text: Forward-looking creation of Leigh Hunt

parts.note: Leigh Hunt published a periodical of essays under a title meaning one who sees the future

explanation.surface: Something visionary invented by the essayist Leigh Hunt.
explanation.walkthrough: Leigh Hunt's essay periodical The Seer (1840) is his creation, and a seer looks forward into the future.
explanation.definitionFit: A prophet sees into the future, and Leigh Hunt used that title for an essay collection.

clue.text: Some early characters of Coppard

parts.note: A. E. Coppard's first story collection was titled with the first couple of Genesis followed by and Pinch Me

explanation.surface: Several characters from the author Coppard's early writing.
explanation.walkthrough: A. E. Coppard's first book was Adam & Eve & Pinch Me (1921); these are early characters both in his career and in human history.
explanation.definitionFit: The first man and woman in Genesis are the earliest characters, and they open the title of Coppard's first book.
